# Why metrics matter 📊 {background-color="#2d4563"}

## Think about this 🤔
### A deceptively simple question

:::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 26px;"}

**Scenario**: You're building a model to predict whether patients have a rare disease that affects [1 in 1,000 people]{.alert}.

Your colleague shows you a model and proudly announces: ["It achieves 99.9% accuracy!"]{.alert}

:::{.fragment}
**Question for you**: Is this model any good?

Take 30 seconds to think about it...
:::

:::{.fragment}
**Hint**: What would happen if the model simply [predicted "no disease" for every single patient]{.alert}?
:::

:::{.fragment}
**The uncomfortable truth**: That "99.9% accurate" model [catches zero actual cases]{.alert}. Every sick patient is missed!
:::
:::

## The accuracy paradox
### When 99% accuracy is terrible

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- This is called the [accuracy paradox]{.alert}
- Accuracy measures [overall correctness]{.alert}, but doesn't tell us:
  - How many sick patients we actually found
  - How many healthy patients we falsely alarmed
  - Whether errors are concentrated in one group
- The problem is especially severe with [class imbalance]{.alert}
- Real examples of imbalanced data:
  - Fraud: [0.2% of transactions]{.alert}
  - Security threats: [< 0.01%]{.alert} of events
  - Manufacturing defects: Often [< 1%]{.alert}
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![The accuracy paradox](figures/accuracy-paradox.png){width="90%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/accuracy-paradox.png"}

Source: [Medium](https://medium.com/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## What are we really measuring?
### Key questions before choosing metrics

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- Every metric captures [one aspect]{.alert} of model performance
- There's no single "best" metric—it depends on [your specific context]{.alert}
- Key questions to ask yourself:
  - What's the cost of a [false positive]{.alert}? (Saying "yes" when it's "no")
  - What's the cost of a [false negative]{.alert}? (Saying "no" when it's "yes")
  - Are the classes [balanced]{.alert} or imbalanced?
  - What [action]{.alert} will be taken based on the prediction?
- The choice of metric is a [design decision with real-world consequences]{.alert}
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Different metrics for different goals](figures/metrics-tradeoffs.png){width="90%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/metrics-tradeoffs.png"}

Source: [Analytics Vidhya](https://www.analyticsvidhya.com/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

# Classification metrics 🎯 {background-color="#2d4563"}

## The confusion matrix
### The foundation of classification evaluation

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- A table showing [all possible prediction outcomes]{.alert}
- Four key quantities:
  - **True Positives (TP)**: Correctly predicted positive
  - **True Negatives (TN)**: Correctly predicted negative
  - **False Positives (FP)**: Predicted positive, but actually negative (Type I error)
  - **False Negatives (FN)**: Predicted negative, but actually positive (Type II error)
- [All classification metrics come from these four numbers!]{.alert}
- Understanding the confusion matrix is [essential]{.alert} for model evaluation
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
| | Predicted + | Predicted − |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| **Actual +** | TP ✅ | FN ❌ |
| **Actual −** | FP ❌ | TN ✅ |

<br>

[![Confusion matrix visualisation](figures/confusion-matrix.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/confusion-matrix.png"}
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Precision
### How trustworthy are positive predictions?

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- **Precision** = TP / (TP + FP)
- In words: [When the model says "yes", how often is it right?]{.alert}
- High precision = [few false alarms]{.alert}
- Important when [false positives are costly]{.alert}:
  - **Spam detection**: Don't want important emails in spam!
  - **Product recommendations**: Don't annoy users with bad suggestions
  - **Fraud prevention**: Don't block legitimate transactions
  - **Child protection**: Don't falsely accuse innocent people
- Trade-off: Being too cautious might mean [missing real positives]{.alert}
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Precision focuses on predicted positives](figures/precision.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/precision.png"}

Source: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Precision_and_recall)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Recall (Sensitivity)
### How many positives did we catch?

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- **Recall** = TP / (TP + FN)
- Also called [sensitivity]{.alert} or [true positive rate]{.alert}
- In words: [Of all actual positives, how many did we find?]{.alert}
- High recall = [we don't miss many positives]{.alert}
- Important when [false negatives are costly]{.alert}:
  - **Disease screening**: Don't miss sick patients!
  - **Security threats**: Don't miss genuine attacks
  - **Safety systems**: Don't miss dangerous situations
  - **Airport security**: Better safe than sorry
- Trade-off: Catching everything might mean [many false alarms]{.alert}
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Recall focuses on actual positives](figures/recall.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/recall.png"}

Source: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Precision_and_recall)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## The precision-recall trade-off
### You can't have it all

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- Most classifiers output a [probability score]{.alert}
- We choose a [threshold]{.alert} to decide "positive" vs "negative"
- Moving the threshold [trades off precision and recall]{.alert}:
  - **High threshold** (strict): Only confident positives → High precision, low recall
  - **Low threshold** (lenient): Accept weak positives → High recall, low precision
- This creates a [precision-recall curve]{.alert}
- The [optimal threshold depends on your application!]{.alert}
- No free lunch: Improving one usually hurts the other
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![The precision-recall trade-off](figures/precision-recall-tradeoff.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/precision-recall-tradeoff.png"}

Source: [Scikit-learn](https://scikit-learn.org/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## F1 score
### Balancing precision and recall

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- What if you care equally about precision and recall?
- **F1 Score** = Harmonic mean of precision and recall
- Formula: F1 = 2 × (Precision × Recall) / (Precision + Recall)
- Why harmonic mean? It [penalises extreme imbalances]{.alert}
  - If either precision or recall is very low, F1 drops significantly
- F1 = 1 is perfect, F1 = 0 is worst
- Very popular for [imbalanced classification]{.alert}

| Precision | Recall | F1 Score |
|-----------|--------|----------|
| 0.80 | 0.80 | **0.80** |
| 0.80 | 0.20 | **0.32** |
| 1.00 | 0.01 | **0.02** |
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![F1 balances precision and recall](figures/f1-score.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/f1-score.png"}

Source: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F-score)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## ROC curves and AUC
### Evaluating across all thresholds

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- **ROC Curve** (Receiver Operating Characteristic):
  - Plots [True Positive Rate]{.alert} vs [False Positive Rate]{.alert}
  - Shows performance across [all possible thresholds]{.alert}
- **AUC** (Area Under Curve):
  - AUC = 0.5 → Random guessing (diagonal line)
  - AUC = 1.0 → Perfect classifier
  - AUC = 0.8+ → Generally considered "good"
- Interpretation: [The probability that a random positive ranks higher than a random negative]{.alert}
- Useful for [comparing models]{.alert} regardless of threshold choice
- Less sensitive to class imbalance than accuracy
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![ROC curve and AUC](figures/roc-curve.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/roc-curve.png"}

Source: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Receiver_operating_characteristic)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Regression metrics
### When the target is continuous

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
- For regression (predicting numbers), we need different metrics:

| Metric | Formula | Intuition |
|--------|---------|-----------|
| **MAE** | Mean of \|actual - predicted\| | Average error size (in original units) |
| **MSE** | Mean of (actual - predicted)² | Average squared error (penalises big errors) |
| **RMSE** | √MSE | Same as MSE, but in original units |
| **R²** | 1 - (SS_res / SS_tot) | Proportion of variance explained |

:::{.fragment}
**Key intuitions:**

- **MAE**: "On average, predictions are off by X units"
- **RMSE**: "Typical error size, but big errors count more"
- **R²**: "The model explains X% of the variation in the data" (R² = 0.8 means 80%)
:::
:::

# Validation & overfitting ⚠️ {background-color="#2d4563"}

## What is overfitting?
### The enemy of generalisation

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- [Overfitting]{.alert}: Model performs well on training data but poorly on new data
- The model has [memorised]{.alert} the training set, including its noise and quirks
- It hasn't learned the [underlying patterns]{.alert}
- Signs of overfitting:
  - [Excellent training performance]{.alert}
  - [Poor test performance]{.alert}
  - Gap grows with model complexity
- Think of it like [memorising exam answers]{.alert} vs understanding the material
- The student who memorises fails when questions are rephrased
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Overfitting visualised](figures/overfitting.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/overfitting.png"}

Source: [Scikit-learn](https://scikit-learn.org/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Underfitting vs overfitting
### Finding the sweet spot

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Underfitting, good fit, and overfitting](figures/overfit-underfit.png){width="75%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/overfit-underfit.png"}
:::

:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=33%}
**Underfitting** 📉

- Model [too simple]{.alert}
- High bias, low variance
- Poor on training AND test
- Hasn't captured the pattern
- Solution: More complex model
:::

:::{.column width=33%}
**Good fit** ✅

- [Right complexity]{.alert}
- Balanced bias and variance
- Good on both sets
- Captures the true pattern
- This is what we want!
:::

:::{.column width=33%}
**Overfitting** 📈

- Model [too complex]{.alert}
- Low bias, high variance
- Great on training, poor on test
- Memorised noise
- Solution: Regularisation
:::
:::
:::

## Train, validation, and test splits
### The three-way split

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- **Training set** (~60-70%): Fit the model
- **Validation set** (~15-20%): Tune hyperparameters, compare models
- **Test set** (~15-20%): [Final evaluation (touch only once!)]{.alert}
- [Never look at test data during model development!]{.alert}
- If you tune on test data, you're [cheating]{.alert}
- The test set must remain [truly unseen]{.alert} until the very end
- Think of it as the [final exam]{.alert}—you shouldn't see the questions while studying
- A common mistake: Using the test set to select models, then reporting "test accuracy"
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Train/validation/test split](figures/train-val-test.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/train-val-test.png"}

Source: [Machine Learning Mastery](https://machinelearningmastery.com/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Cross-validation
### Making the most of limited data

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- With small datasets, a single split may be [unreliable]{.alert}
- **K-fold cross-validation**:
  1. Split data into K equal parts (folds)
  2. Train on K-1 folds, validate on the remaining 1 fold
  3. Repeat K times, rotating which fold is used for validation
  4. Average the K results
- Common choices: K = 5 or K = 10
- Every data point is used for both training and validation
- Gives a more [robust estimate]{.alert} of model performance
- More computationally expensive (train K times)
- [Stratified K-fold]{.alert}: Preserves class proportions in each fold
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![5-fold cross-validation](figures/cross-validation.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/cross-validation.png"}

Source: [Scikit-learn](https://scikit-learn.org/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Preventing overfitting
### Your toolkit

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
| Technique | How it works |
|-----------|--------------|
| **More data** | Harder to memorise larger datasets |
| **Simpler model** | Reduce number of parameters |
| **Regularisation** | Add penalty for complex models (L1, L2) |
| **Early stopping** | Stop training before overfitting occurs |
| **Dropout** | Randomly disable neurons during training |
| **Data augmentation** | Create variations of training examples |
| **Cross-validation** | Detect overfitting early |

> "All models are wrong, but some are useful." — George Box
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Training and validation curves](figures/learning-curves.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/learning-curves.png"}

The gap between training and validation indicates overfitting

Source: [Scikit-learn](https://scikit-learn.org/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

# Evaluating text & language 📝 {background-color="#2d4563"}

## From classification to language generation
### New challenges emerge

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- Classification: [One correct label per input]{.alert}
  - Cat or dog? → "Cat" or "Dog"
- Language generation: [Many valid outputs]{.alert}
  - "The cat sat on the mat" ≈ "A feline rested upon the rug"
  - Both are correct! How do we score them?
- Traditional metrics struggle with this [one-to-many]{.alert} problem
- We need new ways to measure:
  - [Fluency]{.alert}: Is the text grammatical and natural?
  - [Relevance]{.alert}: Does it address the question?
  - [Factuality]{.alert}: Is it actually true?
- This is one of the [hardest problems]{.alert} in AI evaluation
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Language evaluation is hard](figures/metrics-tradeoffs.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/metrics-tradeoffs.png"}

Source: [Analytics Vidhya](https://www.analyticsvidhya.com/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Perplexity
### How surprised is the model?

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- [Perplexity]{.alert} measures how well a language model predicts a text
- Formally: The exponential of the average negative log-likelihood
- Intuition: [How many equally likely words could come next?]{.alert}
  - Perplexity of 10 → Model is as uncertain as choosing from 10 random words
  - Perplexity of 100 → Much more uncertain
- Lower perplexity = model is [more confident]{.alert} about its predictions
- Used to:
  - Compare different language models
  - Track training progress
  - Evaluate fluency
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
**Example:**

"The capital of France is ___"

- "Paris" → Low perplexity ✅
- "elephant" → High perplexity ❌

<br>

**The big limitation:**

"The earth is ___"

- "flat" → Could have [low perplexity]{.alert}!

Perplexity measures [fluency, not truthfulness]{.alert}. A confident lie still has low perplexity.
:::
:::
:::
:::

## BLEU score
### Measuring translation quality

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- **BLEU** (Bilingual Evaluation Understudy)
- Developed at IBM in 2002 for machine translation
- Counts [n-gram matches]{.alert} between output and reference translations
- n-grams: sequences of n words
  - 1-gram: "the", "cat", "sat"
  - 2-gram: "the cat", "cat sat"
- Focuses on [precision]{.alert}: What fraction of generated words match the reference?
- Includes a [brevity penalty]{.alert} for short outputs
- Score from 0 to 1 (or 0 to 100)
- BLEU > 30: Understandable; BLEU > 60: Excellent
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
**Example:**

Reference: "The cat sat on the mat"

Output A: "The cat sat on the mat"
→ BLEU = 1.0 ✅

Output B: "A cat was sitting on a mat"
→ BLEU ≈ 0.25 (low despite good meaning!)

Output C: "The mat sat on the cat"
→ BLEU ≈ 0.8 (high despite wrong meaning!)

<br>

[Word overlap ≠ Semantic correctness]{.alert}
:::
:::
:::
:::

## ROUGE score
### Measuring summary quality

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- **ROUGE** (Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation)
- Designed for [text summarisation]{.alert}
- Focuses on [recall]{.alert}: What fraction of reference words appear in the output?
- Several variants:
  - **ROUGE-1**: Unigram overlap
  - **ROUGE-2**: Bigram overlap
  - **ROUGE-L**: Longest common subsequence
- Strengths:
  - Simple and fast to compute
  - Correlates reasonably with human judgment
  - Widely used as a baseline
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
**Limitations of BLEU & ROUGE:**

- Don't understand [meaning]{.alert}
- Penalise valid [paraphrases]{.alert}
- Can't detect [factual errors]{.alert}
- Favour [copying]{.alert} over abstraction

**Example:**

Reference: "The president announced new policies"

Good summary: "New governmental measures were revealed"
→ Low ROUGE (few matching words)

Bad summary: "The president the president the"
→ Higher ROUGE (more matches!)

[We need better evaluation methods for modern AI]{.alert}
:::
:::
:::
:::

# Hallucinations 🎭 {background-color="#2d4563"}

## What are hallucinations?
### When AI confidently makes things up

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- [Hallucination]{.alert}: AI output that is fluent but factually incorrect or fabricated
- The model generates plausible-sounding content that [isn't grounded in reality]{.alert}
- Common forms:
  - **Fabricated citations**: Inventing papers that don't exist
  - **Made-up statistics**: "73% of scientists agree..."
  - **False biographical details**: Wrong dates, events, achievements
  - **Confident nonsense**: Eloquent explanations of things that are simply wrong
- [This is one of the biggest challenges]{.alert} in deploying language models
- Why? Because they're trained to predict [likely text]{.alert}, not [true text]{.alert}
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Hallucinations in AI](figures/data-leakage.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/data-leakage.png"}

**The core problem:**

Models optimise for:

`P(next word | context)`

Not for:

`P(statement is true)`

Source: [MIT DCAI](https://dcai.csail.mit.edu/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Real-world consequences
### Why hallucinations matter

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
**Notable incidents (all real!):**

- ⚖️ **Legal** (2023): Two lawyers submitted a brief citing [six non-existent cases]{.alert} generated by ChatGPT. They were sanctioned by the court.
- 🏥 **Medical**: AI chatbots have provided [dangerous health advice]{.alert} citing fabricated studies
- 📰 **News**: AI-generated fake news stories have [moved stock prices]{.alert}
- 📚 **Academic**: Students have submitted essays with [entirely invented references]{.alert}
- 🔬 **Science**: Researchers have found fake citations in published papers

**The stakes are rising:**

- More people trusting AI outputs without verification
- Harder for non-experts to spot fabrications
- Legal and reputational risks for organisations
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}

**Discussion question:**

How would you verify if an AI's answer is correct?

- Check primary sources?
- Ask another AI?
- Trust your intuition?
- Rely on reputation of the AI company?

<br>

[Critical thinking remains essential]{.alert}

<br>

🎬 Watch: [IBM Explains AI Hallucinations](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cfqtFvWOfg0) (5 min)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Detecting and mitigating hallucinations
### Approaches and tools

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
**Detection methods:**

- **Manual verification**: Human fact-checkers (gold standard but expensive)
- **LLM-as-a-Judge**: Use one model to evaluate another
- **Consistency checks**: Ask the same question multiple ways
- **Cross-referencing**: Check against knowledge bases
- **Retrieval-based verification**: Look up claims in trusted sources

**Mitigation strategies:**

- [Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)]{.alert}: Ground answers in retrieved documents
- Chain-of-thought prompting with citations
- Fine-tuning on high-quality, verified data
- Teaching models to say "I don't know"
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
**RAG: A quick preview**

Instead of relying on "memory", [look things up]{.alert}:

1. User asks a question
2. System retrieves relevant documents
3. Model generates answer based on retrieved context
4. Answer includes citations to sources

[We'll cover RAG in detail in a future lecture!]{.alert}

# Benchmarks & leaderboards 🏆 {background-color="#2d4563"}

## What are AI benchmarks?
### Standardised tests for AI systems

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- [Benchmarks]{.alert}: Standardised datasets and tasks to compare AI models
- Like academic exams, but for AI systems
- Famous examples:
  - **MMLU**: 57 subjects of academic knowledge (maths, history, law...)
  - **HellaSwag**: Commonsense reasoning
  - **TruthfulQA**: Resistance to common misconceptions
  - **HumanEval**: Code generation ability
  - **MATH**: Mathematical problem-solving
- Enable [objective comparison]{.alert} across different models
- Drive progress by setting clear, measurable targets
- Help track capability improvements over time
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![AI benchmarks](figures/class-imbalance.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/class-imbalance.png"}

Source: [MIT DCAI](https://dcai.csail.mit.edu/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## The leaderboard culture
### Racing to the top

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- Public leaderboards rank models by benchmark scores
- [Hugging Face Open LLM Leaderboard]{.alert} is hugely influential
- Benefits:
  - Encourages [transparency]{.alert}
  - Enables [fair comparison]{.alert}
  - Tracks [progress]{.alert} over time
  - Creates healthy [competition]{.alert}
- Risks:
  - [Overfitting to benchmarks]{.alert} rather than real capability
  - [Gaming]{.alert} through benchmark contamination
  - Neglecting capabilities that aren't measured

**Try it yourself:** [huggingface.co/spaces/HuggingFaceH4/open_llm_leaderboard](https://huggingface.co/spaces/HuggingFaceH4/open_llm_leaderboard)
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Hugging Face Leaderboard](figures/slice-performance.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/slice-performance.png"}

Source: [MIT DCAI](https://dcai.csail.mit.edu/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## The dark side of benchmarks
### When metrics become targets

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
[Goodhart's Law]{.alert}: "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure"

**Common problems:**

- **Benchmark contamination**: Test data accidentally (or intentionally) appears in training data—the model memorises rather than generalises
- **Teaching to the test**: Teams optimise for benchmark quirks rather than genuine capability
- **Metric saturation**: Models achieve "human-level" on benchmarks but still fail in real-world scenarios
- **Narrow focus**: Only measuring what's easy to measure

**What benchmarks often miss:**

- Real-world robustness and edge cases
- Safety and alignment
- Creative problem-solving
- Long-horizon reasoning
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Goodhart's Law in action](figures/goodharts-law.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/goodharts-law.png"}

Source: [Thomas & Uminsky (2022)](https://www.cell.com/patterns/fulltext/S2666-3899(22)00056-3)
:::
:::
:::
:::

# Ethics beyond accuracy 🤔 {background-color="#2d4563"}

## Fairness: When overall accuracy hides problems
### The disaggregation imperative

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- Overall accuracy can hide [serious failures for specific groups]{.alert}
- **Real example** (Buolamwini & Gebru, 2018):
  - Commercial face recognition error rates:
  - Light-skinned men: [0.8% error]{.alert}
  - Dark-skinned women: [34.7% error]{.alert}
  - 43× worse performance for one group!
- This is called [data slicing]{.alert} or [subgroup analysis]{.alert}
- The model "works" overall, but [fails for specific populations]{.alert}
- Even removing sensitive features doesn't help—they [correlate with other features]{.alert}
- [Always evaluate models per subgroup, not just overall]{.alert}
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Subgroup performance disparities](figures/slice-performance.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/slice-performance.png"}

Source: [MIT DCAI](https://dcai.csail.mit.edu/2024/data-centric-evaluation/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Fairness metrics
### Quantifying equity

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
**Key fairness metrics:**

- **Demographic parity**: Equal positive prediction rates across groups
- **Equalised odds**: Equal TPR and FPR across groups
- **Predictive parity**: Equal precision across groups

**The impossibility theorem:**

[You cannot satisfy all fairness criteria simultaneously]{.alert} (except in special cases)

- This is a mathematical fact, not a failure of effort
- Different metrics encode different [values and trade-offs]{.alert}
- Choice of fairness metric is ultimately a [value judgment]{.alert}
- There's no "correct" answer—it depends on context and stakeholders
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Fairness in ML](figures/fairness-metrics.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/fairness-metrics.png"}

Source: [Google AI](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/fairness-overview)
:::
:::
:::
:::

## Distribution shift
### When the world changes

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
- Models are trained on [historical data]{.alert}
- But the real world [changes over time]{.alert}
- [Distribution shift]{.alert}: Mismatch between training and deployment data

**Three types:**

1. **Covariate shift**: Inputs change (model trained in SF, deployed in Boston)
2. **Concept shift**: Relationships change (what predicted fraud in 2010 ≠ 2025)
3. **Label shift**: Class frequencies change (COVID test positivity rates)

**Solutions:**

- Monitor performance continuously
- Retrain when metrics degrade
- Use [robust validation]{.alert} strategies
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
:::{style="text-align: center;"}
[![Distribution shift example](figures/distribution-shift.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/distribution-shift.png"}

Source: [MIT DCAI](https://dcai.csail.mit.edu/2023/imbalance-outliers-shift/)
:::
:::
:::
:::

# Practical considerations 🛠️ {background-color="#2d4563"}

## Choosing the right metrics
### A decision framework

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}

| Question | If yes... |
|----------|-----------|
| Is false positive cost high? | Prioritise [precision]{.alert} |
| Is false negative cost high? | Prioritise [recall]{.alert} |
| Are classes imbalanced? | Use [F1 or AUC]{.alert}, not accuracy |
| Is it a generation task? | Need [text-specific metrics]{.alert} + human eval |
| Are multiple groups affected? | Check [fairness metrics]{.alert} per group |
| Will data change over time? | Plan for [distribution shift]{.alert} monitoring |

:::{.fragment}
**Golden rule:** [No single metric is sufficient]{.alert}

Use a [dashboard of complementary measures]{.alert} that capture different aspects of performance.
:::
:::

## Building your evaluation strategy
### Putting it all together

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 22px;"}
:::{.columns}
:::{.column width=55%}
**A practical framework:**

1. **Define success** — What does "good enough" mean for your use case?
2. **Choose primary metrics** — Based on the cost of different errors
3. **Add secondary metrics** — Fairness, latency, cost, interpretability
4. **Set up monitoring** — Track performance over time
5. **Plan for failure** — What happens when metrics degrade?
6. **Document everything** — Why these metrics? What are the known limitations?

**Remember:**

- Start simple, iterate
- Involve stakeholders in metric selection
- Metrics shape incentives—choose wisely
:::

:::{.column width=45%}
**Example dashboard:**

| Metric | Value | Status |
|--------|-------|--------|
| F1 (overall) | 0.87 | ✅ |
| F1 (group A) | 0.89 | ✅ |
| F1 (group B) | 0.71 | ⚠️ |
| Latency (p95) | 120ms | ✅ |
| Fairness gap | 18% | ⚠️ |

<br>

[Evaluation is ongoing, not one-time]{.alert}

[Monitor, don't just measure]{.alert}
:::
:::
:::

# Summary ✅ {background-color="#2d4563"}

## Main takeaways

:::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 24px;"}

- `r fa('exclamation-triangle')` [Accuracy alone is dangerous]{.alert}—especially for imbalanced classes

- `r fa('balance-scale')` [Precision vs recall]{.alert} trade-off depends on the cost of different errors

- `r fa('chart-line')` [Validation is essential]{.alert}—never evaluate on training data, beware overfitting

- `r fa('language')` [Text evaluation is hard]{.alert}—BLEU and ROUGE measure overlap, not meaning

- `r fa('ghost')` [Hallucinations]{.alert} are a fundamental challenge—we'll explore more in a later lecture

- `r fa('trophy')` [Benchmarks help but can mislead]{.alert}—beware of Goodhart's Law

- `r fa('users')` [Fairness requires]{.alert} looking beyond aggregate metrics to subgroup performance
:::
